chunks: "I'd attack it in order of cheapness.

First, minimize the time the body diode conducts: use adaptive or predictive dead time and a strong gate driver so the gap is just enough to avoid shoot-through, say 10 to 20 nanoseconds instead of 50.
That cuts conduction loss directly and also cuts the stored charge, so it reduces recovery loss too. Second, put a Schottky in parallel with the low-side FET. At about 0.
4 volts it conducts instead of the 0. 75 volts body diode, and it has almost no recovery charge.
The catch is the loop inductance: the current has to commutate into the Schottky in a nanosecond or so, and a nanohenry of lead inductance costs a volt, so the body diode would conduct first.
That's why it's done inside the package or on the die, as in monolithic Schottky-integrated FETs, not as a separate part a centimeter away.
Third, pick the FET for low Q rr and soft recovery, not just low R DS(on) . A few nC saved at 12 volts and 1 megahertz can beat a milliohm of resistance.
Fourth, tame the spike: a gate or boot resistor on the high-side turn-on to slow di over dt , or an RC snubber, and tight layout.
Those fix ringing and EMI but cost some efficiency. And finally, device choices: GaN has no recovery charge but a higher reverse drop, so dead time must be very short."
